title: Mixed conditionals
tagline: One sentence, two moments: a past cause with a present result, or the other way round.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (would / had)
Writing Part 1 — essay: consequences and regrets
why: The second and third conditionals each stay inside one time. Real life doesn't: a decision you made years ago explains where you are today, and the person you are now explains what you did last week. B2 First tests exactly this crossing of times, usually in Part 4, where the key word is often would, had or if.

diagrams.title: Past cause → present result

marks.label: She didn't take the job in Lima.

diagrams.caption: If she had taken the job, she would be living in Lima now.

diagrams.title: Present state → past result

marks.label: He didn't drive us to the match yesterday.

diagrams.caption: If he weren't such a nervous driver, he would have driven us yesterday.

rows.label: Example
cells: If I had studied, I would have passed.
If I had studied, I would be at university now.
If I were more organised, I would have passed.

head: Pattern
If-clause
Result clause
What it means
rows: an imaginary past change with a result you can see now
would / could / might have + past participle
a permanent or present fact that explains a past event

use.point: A past decision or event with a result you feel now

examples.text: If Nadia had joined the robotics club last year, she would know how to code by now.
If we hadn't missed the early bus, we wouldn't be standing in the rain.
If my grandparents hadn't moved to Arequipa, I might not speak Spanish at home.

use.point: A present state, habit or personality that explains something in the past

examples.text: If Liam were more patient, he wouldn't have deleted the whole project.
If I didn't live so far from school, I would have stayed for the rehearsal.
If she spoke German, she could have applied for the exchange.
examples.note: could have = ability that was missing

use.point: Regrets and blame, especially in conversation

examples.text: If you had told me the truth, I wouldn't be so angry with you.
If Mateo hadn't lent me his notes, I would be completely lost in this topic.
examples.note: a positive past action, and its present effect

examples.text: If I were a morning person, I would have set three alarms — not one.

use.point: In essays: consequences of policies and habits

examples.text: If the city had invested in cycle lanes ten years ago, traffic would be far lighter today.
If people cared more about recycling, the river would not have reached this state.
examples.note: present attitude → past result; formal register with no contractions

watch_out.wrong: If I would have known about the concert, I would be there now.
watch_out.right: If I had known about the concert, I would be there now.
watch_out.why: No would in the if-clause. The condition takes the past perfect.

watch_out.wrong: If she had studied medicine, she would have been a doctor now.
watch_out.right: If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.
watch_out.why: Now tells you the result is present, so use would + infinitive, not would have.

watch_out.wrong: If he was taller, he would have made the team.
watch_out.right: If he were taller, he would have made the team.
watch_out.why: In unreal conditions use were for all persons — it is the form the exam expects.

watch_out.wrong: If I hadn't lost my phone, I would have been able to call you now.
watch_out.right: If I hadn't lost my phone, I would be able to call you now.
watch_out.why: The result is happening now, so the result clause stays in the present.

watch_out.wrong: If you would be more careful, you wouldn't have broken it.
watch_out.right: If you were more careful, you wouldn't have broken it.
watch_out.why: The present-state condition takes the past simple, never would.

dialogue.title: The science fair that almost wasn't
dialogue.context: Sofia and Liam are waiting outside the hall for the science fair results. Their project nearly missed the deadline.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: If you had backed up the files on Sunday, we wouldn't be this nervous right now.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I know, I know. And if I weren't so disorganised, I would have done it without you asking.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Well, Mateo saved us. If he hadn't stayed up until two, we wouldn't have a project to present today.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: True. If he didn't like coding so much, he would have gone home at ten like everyone else.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And if Miss Vega hadn't given us an extra day, we would be sitting in the audience instead of waiting for results.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Honestly, if I were her, I wouldn't have said yes. We asked at the last minute.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Look, they're opening the doors. If we hadn't rebuilt the model last night, I wouldn't feel this confident.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Confident? If you were really confident, you wouldn't have checked the poster six times this morning.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Seven. Come on — whatever happens, we're here.

items.sentence: If they had left earlier, they ___ here by now.
items.why: by now = a present result → would + infinitive

items.sentence: If I ___ so busy this term, I would have joined the drama club.
items.why: a present state (this term) that explains a past decision → past simple

items.sentence: If she hadn't moved to Cusco, she ___ Quechua today.
If Mateo ___ a better swimmer, he would have entered the race last week.
items.why: a permanent ability explains a past choice → were

items.sentence: We ___ lost now if you had brought the map.
If you ___ my messages last night, you'd know where to meet us.

summary: A mixed conditional joins two different times in one sentence.
Past cause → present result: if + past perfect, would + infinitive (often with now, today, by now).
Present state → past result: if + past simple, would have + past participle (often a personality or a permanent fact).
Never put would in the if-clause, and use were for every person.
In Part 4, the key word (would, had, were) usually tells you which half of the sentence you are rewriting.
